title: The Angel of Death With the Proud King and the Devout Man (Português)

full_text:
In ancient times reigned a mighty monarch who possessed an army of a hundred thousand armored horsemen, treasuries filled with rubies, and palaces of polished jasper. One morning, the king mounted his proudest war-steed, caparisoned in gold-embroidered velvet, and rode out to review his troops, his chest swollen with pride as his heralds blew silver trumpets and the soldiers prostrated themselves before him.

As he rode through the city gates, an elderly traveler dressed in tattered rags stepped into his path, seized the horse’s bridle, and called out: 'Hold, O King! I have a secret word to deliver unto your ear.'

The king frowned in fury, his eyes flashing: 'How dare you touch the royal bridle, insolent beggar? Wait until I return to my palace!'

The stranger answered with calm, terrifying authority: 'My errand cannot wait; it touches your very breath.' He whispered his identity into the king's ear: 'I am the Angel of Death, sent to take your soul this very hour!'

The king turned pale as ashes; his knees shook, his pride vanished like mist, and he stammered: 'Grant me but one hour! Let me return to my palace, bid farewell to my children, and distribute my hoarded gold to the poor!'

The Angel replied: 'Your days were numbered, yet you spent them in pride and oppression, ignoring the cries of the needy. The hour has struck, and not a single breath can be added.' The king collapsed from his saddle, lifeless upon the stones, his gold and armies powerless to save him.

The Angel then traveled to a modest hut outside the city where an honest water-carrier lay dying. The humble man had spent his life distributing water to travelers and sharing his crust with the hungry.

When the Angel appeared, the humble man smiled with peaceful joy: 'Welcome, gentle messenger! I have longed for this hour, for I have lived with clean hands and a loving heart.' His spirit departed gently as a sigh of spring, proving that righteousness alone provides safe passage to eternity.
moral: Earthly pomp and iron armies cannot halt the appointed hour; only a life of justice and humble charity endures. [PT]
